claims.text: Rapid containerless laser melting, high-speed DSC, and CALPHAD can jointly determine melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties for HEAs.
Conventional cast or pre-alloyed HEA ingots typically contain microstructural inhomogeneities.
Containerless processing can overcome microstructural inhomogeneities in HEA ingots.
Small HEA samples can be levitated in flowing argon and heated with a laser in a containerless environment.
High-speed DSC can continuously monitor a containerlessly levitated, laser-heated HEA sample during melting.
Containerless melting and rapid solidification minimize interactions between the HEA and container walls.
Processing under inert argon minimizes oxide formation during HEA melting.
Reduced container interaction and oxidation ensure that measured thermal transitions represent intrinsic HEA properties.
High-speed DSC captures precise melting endotherms even at rapid heating rates.
CALPHAD databases can use thermal signatures to quantitatively extract melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change.
Zinkevich developed an openly available CALPHAD-type database for rare-earth sesquioxides that includes assessments involving fusion enthalpy and volume change on melting.
The proposed method will determine HEA melting temperatures to within ±5–10 °C.
The proposed method will determine HEA fusion enthalpy and entropy to within ±5–10% of expected or calculated values.
HEAs measured by the method are expected to undergo a 2.5–3.1% volume contraction on melting.
The stated accuracy and efficiency will apply across a compositionally diverse HEA family.
Prior CALPHAD work on rare-earth oxides and containerless laser-heating work on HEAs establish the individual feasibility of parts of the proposed workflow.
Prior high-speed DSC studies on similar complex alloys demonstrate reliable extraction of the proposed thermodynamic quantities.
The approach is applicable to HEAs that can be melted without significant oxidation or decomposition.
High reactivity, vaporization, decomposition, and overlapping or complex phase transitions may reduce the effectiveness of the approach.
High-temperature XRD unit-cell refinements can independently quantify the total volume change during melting.
